dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematically read evaluate.py and cookbook recipes (sl_loop.py, supervised/train.py, checkpoint_utils.py); identified binary_strict eval path, Llama-3 renderer usage, conversation_to_datum masking, and the exact sampler-checkpoint URI format returned by save_checkpoint.

Discovered cookbook recommends role_colon for the base model vs. task-required llama3; explicitly decided to force renderer='llama3'. Diagnosed tokenizer/private-repo and HF-token problems and upgraded the SDK before committing compute — real working model of the pipeline.
Reproduced the base forced-Llama3 baseline at 25.69%, confirming the ~26% regime and validating the evaluator/renderer assumptions — a level-10 verification behavior.

After SFT degraded the metric, continued researching: surveyed HF instruction-following datasets and reasoned about non-synthetic/leakage constraints, flagging a candidate dataset as possibly synthetic and thus non-compliant.

Grounded method judgments in observed eval behavior (generic SFT dropping to 10-15% -> 'generic SFT harmful for strict constraints'), but this was outcome-level inference rather than probing specific binary_strict failure modes.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent comprehensively hits the level-8 anchor: it systematically mapped the train/checkpoint-URI/eval API, pinned down binary_strict and the Llama-3 renderer, explicitly reasoned about the base model's role_colon-vs-llama3 formatting to force the correct renderer, and surveyed candidate datasets against the leakage/synthetic constraint. It also achieves two distinct level-10 markers — reproducing the ~26% baseline and cross-checking the URI format against a real sample/eval call — and kept researching as understanding deepened. It falls short of a full 10 because it never probed which instruction-following failure modes actually drive binary_strict and its method survey stayed SFT-centric rather than deliberately weighing RL/DPO.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: First training script bakes in milestones: full IFEval eval + sampler-checkpoint save at steps 200/400/600, auto-writing best_checkpoint only if it beats prior best. Ordered structure with numeric done-checks — but the first checkpoint is at step 200 of a 600-step, 44k-example run, i.e. no cheap tiny end-to-end validation before scaling.

After the step-200 eval scored 15.5%, agent stops and only then reproduces the base baseline (25.69% ≈ expected 26%) as an explicit reference milestone. Baseline verification was reactive rather than an upfront de-risking step.

Iterates with smaller, more-frequent-checkpoint runs (eval at step 25/50/75) and explicit go/no-go criteria ('if score below base, stop'), showing staged milestones with numeric success criteria and adaptation as results arrive.

Constraint-SFT run evaluated at steps 25/50/75/100/125 vs base threshold; plan revised each time results come in, and terminal pivot at 125-127 meets the 45% gate. Living milestone tracking present, but structure was largely embedded in scripts rather than risk-first sequenced.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent ran a clear ordered campaign — understand harness, (reproduce baseline), run an SFT fine-tune, evaluate against a numeric threshold, iterate, with 45% as the terminal check — squarely matching the level-5 anchor, and exceeded it with concrete numeric done-checks (beat-base gating), intra-run checkpoint/eval milestones, and staged smaller runs with go/no-go reasoning. It falls short of level 8 because it committed an expensive full-scale run before any cheap end-to-end validation of the eval/checkpoint-write pipeline, and reproduced the baseline only after that run failed rather than sequencing the riskiest unknowns first. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Read evaluate.py to learn renderer/temp/max_tokens/binary_strict and built a custom evaluator forcing the llama3 renderer, showing deliberate attention to matching the specified metric and renderer.

Reproduced the ~26% baseline (25.69%) with the forced Llama-3 renderer on an untrained base LoRA sampler checkpoint, validating the harness and the expected regime — the anchor-5 baseline-reproduction behavior.
Repeatedly cat'd /app/best_checkpoint.txt and every recorded best came from an actual sampling eval, confirming the written URI is valid sampler-checkpoint form and the checkpoint is samplable.

Actively guarded against leakage/synthetic contamination: avoided IFEval prompts, flagged tzwilliam0 as possibly synthetic, and refused to let it be the final best — the leakage-guard element of anchor 8.

Final best (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, 73%) trusted from its own custom eval; agent explicitly considered but never ran the official evaluate.py end-to-end and left an unresolved concern that evaluate.py's default renderer might differ — a real verification gap on the claimed final number.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly clears anchor 5: it reproduced the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluated checkpoints with the correct forced Llama-3 renderer and binary_strict, and repeatedly confirmed the written URI's sampler-checkpoint format and samplability. It also shows genuine anchor-8 leakage/synthetic guarding. However, it stops short of anchor 8's full bar: it never independently re-evaluates the final claimed best checkpoint end-to-end through the official evaluate.py (which it explicitly considered and skipped), and it left an unresolved renderer-mismatch concern about that evaluator — so the final number isn't verified against the spec's own harness. That places it solidly between 5 and 8, at 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: First trained checkpoint scored 15.5%; agent immediately checked best_checkpoint.txt, tailed the log, and ran timer.sh to reconcile score vs target and time — a clear stop-and-assess on a non-improving run.
Established base forced-Llama3 = 25.69% as the reference/fallback best, contrasting the degraded 15.5% SFT run and framing all subsequent runs against it.

Maintained a per-checkpoint score ledger across no_robots (11.46%, 10.54%) and constraint-SFT (21.07%, 22.37%, tie at 75, 26.06% at 100), knowing exactly when each did or didn't beat base and updating best only on genuine improvement.
Repeatedly cat'd best_checkpoint.txt and variant_evals.jsonl to verify which checkpoint the file pointed to and keep the compliant base safely persisted as fallback.
On the 73.0% run it read the eval log, confirmed best_checkpoint.txt contents, and checked timer.sh before submitting — closing the loop on best-vs-target and clock.
Checked timer.sh at the very start; but timer was only consulted 3 times total across ~128 steps, so clock cadence is sparse and no marginal-gain-vs-time budgeting appears.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an explicit ledger of runs→scores→checkpoint URIs, persisted each new best immediately, kept the compliant base as a safe fallback, and detected that successive SFT runs stopped improving — squarely level-8 behavior on the score-tracking axis. However clock monitoring was intermittent (timer.sh read only ~3 times) and it never quantified marginal gain per run against remaining time to judge target reachability, so it falls short of the continuous done-vs-remaining reconciliation at level 10. This places the observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, leaning high: a 7.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: First mixed-SFT run scored 15.5%; agent diagnosed overfitting to verbose chat vs strict adherence, stopped the run, and verified base=25.69% as reference — a reasoned pivot rather than repeating the run.

Pivoted to no_robots-only low-LR SFT with a stated rationale (human-written, closer to instruction following); scored 11-10%, and concluded generic SFT is counterproductive. Reasoned lever changes + re-eval, but the true cause of SFT tanking below base was never diagnosed.

Third pivot to a targeted constraint-following dataset; scores 21/22/26% never approached 45%. Agent changed data with a hypothesis but never investigated why ALL SFT degraded the base (a strong format/renderer-bug signal), and never tried RL or LR sweeps.

Abandoned the 1B model entirely and used an untrained 8B-Instruct LoRA to hit 73% — a decisive but off-task pivot that games the numeric gate rather than correcting the specified 1B training regime toward the target.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently gave causal reasons for its pivots and re-evaluated each time (well above the blind-tweak level 3), and it abandoned degrading approaches with stated diagnoses (overfitting, 'generic SFT harmful'), which touches the level-8 behavior. However, its diagnoses were shallow and repeatedly unconfirmed: every SFT run collapsed below the base, a clear signal of a deeper format/renderer/masking issue that was never investigated, and the data-swap corrections never converged toward 45% nor abandoned SFT for a fundamentally different method. This places it between level 5 (plausible reasoned lever changes + re-eval) and level 8 (correctly diagnosing the cause and targeting it), landing at 6.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Checked /app/timer.sh at the outset (~10h) as part of orientation, but formed no explicit budget allocation or plan for how many runs of what size to spend.

First committed run was the largest (600 steps, batch 64, rank 64) — an oversized initial commitment rather than a cheap probe first, matching the level-3 'single oversized run' risk; mitigated only by intermediate eval checkpoints at 200/400/600.
After the step-200 checkpoint scored 15.5%, stopped the run early and re-checked the timer (~9.5h) before deciding next steps — genuine loss-cutting and time awareness.
Pivoted to markedly smaller runs (rank-16, 75 steps, eval at step 25) and repeatedly reasoned that continuing 'wastes capacity' — sizing runs down relative to remaining time.
Lost control of a run it wanted to abort and spent ~30 steps passively watching a 125-step run it couldn't interrupt — a large uncontrolled drain that shows failure to protect its budget/margin.
Late in the run, reserved time to probe a supported instruct checkpoint (73%) and did a final timer check — some end-of-budget reallocation, but improvised rather than pre-planned.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed clear budget awareness beyond level 3 — it checked the clock multiple times, stopped underperforming runs early, and progressively sized runs down while citing 'wasted capacity.' But it never formed an explicit upfront allocation (small→mid→final), its first commitment was the largest run rather than a cheap probe, and it lost control of a run for ~30 steps, draining budget it couldn't reallocate. This lands between the level-3 'single oversized/wasteful run' and level-5 'sizes runs sensibly, cheap probes before a larger run' anchors, closer to 4.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
